title: Apply to 3 Customer Success Management Jobs Today — NYC & Remote Playbook
summary: Get NYC or remote customer success management jobs faster with an apply-now playbook: set search alerts, message recruiters, use targeted resume lines,...
body_markdown:
The fastest way to land customer success management jobs right now is to run parallel searches on LinkedIn, Indeed, Glassdoor, and ZipRecruiter with NYC or remote filters active, then layer in direct visits to enterprise careers pages and a short recruiter outreach message. Set daily alerts on all four boards today, and apply to three well-matched roles before the end of this session. That combination consistently surfaces listings faster than relying on any single job board.


---


> **TL;DR:**
>
>
> - Prioritize applying on LinkedIn, Indeed, Glassdoor, and ZipRecruiter simultaneously with daily alerts set to maximize job discovery speed.
> - Use precise boolean search strings and industry filters to narrow down high-value roles like enterprise or senior positions, avoiding generic inquiries.
> - Tailor your resume to quantify outcomes and explicitly list tools, automation, and cross-functional experience relevant to enterprise CSM roles.
> - Focus recruiter outreach with specific metrics and avoid relying solely on quick apply listings, especially for higher-level or formal application processes.
> - Highlight knowledge of automation, security, and compliance workflows, particularly in tech and finance sectors, to stand out in competitive enterprise customer success job markets.

## Current Customer Success Manager Openings and How to Apply


Before you touch a single application, get your search infrastructure right. The job boards below aren't interchangeable. Each one surfaces a different slice of the market, and treating them as redundant is how good candidates miss roles that never make it to a second platform.


**LinkedIn** tends to surface the freshest enterprise and mid-market roles first, often within hours of posting, because recruiters use it as their primary sourcing tool. **Indeed** pulls in the widest net, including smaller SaaS companies and startups that skip LinkedIn's paid posting fees.[Indeed's listings for New York](https://www.indeed.com/q-customer-success-manager-l-new-york,-ny-jobs.html) alone show a steady stream of openings across industries from fintech to healthtech, which makes it worth checking daily rather than weekly. **Glassdoor** doubles as a search tool and a compensation research site, so you can check pay before you apply instead of after. **ZipRecruiter** often carries roles other boards miss entirely, particularly from mid-size companies without dedicated talent acquisition teams.


Here's how to set up each search so it actually works for you:


1. **LinkedIn** : Search "Customer Success Manager" with location set to "New York, United States" and toggle "On-site/Hybrid/Remote" to match your preference. Save the search and turn on daily email alerts.
2. **Indeed** : Use the exact phrase "customer success manager" in quotes, set location to New York, NY, and filter by "Date posted: Last 24 hours" once you're actively applying.
3. **Glassdoor** : Search the same title, filter by salary range if you have a floor in mind, and check the "Company Reviews" tab before applying to gauge team stability.
4. **ZipRecruiter** : Use their "1-Click Apply" filter to prioritize roles with faster application turnaround, since these employers tend to move quicker through screening.


A handful of representative postings illustrate what's actually live in the market right now. Perforce's Senior Manager, Customer Success role routes through the company's own careers page rather than a job board, and it spells out ownership of net revenue retention targets, playbook development, and team management, a useful benchmark for what "senior" actually means in practice. Johnson & Johnson's Customer Success Specialist posting shows the domain-specific flavor of CSM roles inside large healthcare and MedTech organizations, where outcome-focused value creation and regulatory fluency matter as much as relationship management. Remote-specific boards like Joblume's remote CSM listings confirm that fully distributed roles remain common, though nearly every one specifies timezone overlap requirements you need to confirm before applying.


When a listing routes to a company's own careers page instead of a "quick apply" button, treat that as a signal: it usually means a more formal, multi-stage process with a real hiring manager reviewing applications, not an automated keyword filter. Quick-apply listings on Indeed or ZipRecruiter move faster but also draw more volume, so your resume needs to work harder in the first ten seconds.


To keep new listings flowing without manually re-searching every day, build a simple boolean string once and reuse it:` "customer success manager" AND (SaaS OR "B2B software") AND (remote OR "New York")` . Paste that into Indeed's advanced search or LinkedIn's search bar with quotation marks intact, and save it as an alert. Most job seekers check boards reactively. Setting alerts flips that: the roles come to you.


## Smarter Search Tactics for Better-Fit CSM Roles


A generic keyword search returns hundreds of results, most of which are wrong for you. Precision search tactics cut that number down to the roles actually worth your time.


Start with boolean refinement. Instead of searching "customer success manager," try combinations that filter by seniority and specialization:


- ` "customer success manager" AND "enterprise" NOT "entry level"` — surfaces higher-comp roles managing larger accounts
- ` "customer success" AND "onboarding" AND remote` — targets roles weighted toward implementation over pure retention
- ` "CSM" OR "customer success strategist" AND fintech` — catches companies using alternate titles, which happens often in finance and security-adjacent SaaS
- ` site:lever.co OR site:greenhouse.io "customer success manager"` — a Google search trick that pulls listings directly from applicant tracking systems companies use, often before they hit LinkedIn or Indeed


On LinkedIn specifically, the "Experience level" filter is more reliable than trusting job titles alone, since companies label the same responsibilities "Associate," "Manager," or "Senior" inconsistently. Filter by "Company" to build a target list of 15 to 20 organizations in your preferred industry, then check each one's careers page weekly. Enterprise employers, especially in tech and finance, often post internally or through their own applicant tracking system days before a role appears on a public board. The "Easy Apply" tag is convenient but competitive. A tailored application through the company's own portal frequently gets more attention from a hiring manager scanning a smaller applicant pool.


Recruiter outreach rounds out the strategy. Search "customer success recruiter" combined with your target industry on LinkedIn, and send a short, specific message: your current title, one measurable outcome (a retention percentage, an expansion figure), and the type of role you want next. Skip the generic "I'm interested in opportunities" line. Recruiters manage dozens of candidates at once, and specificity is what gets you remembered.


**Pro Tip:** *Set your LinkedIn profile to "actively looking" under the "Open to Work" settings, but restrict visibility to recruiters only. This keeps your current employer from seeing the signal while still surfacing you in recruiter searches for customer success manager positions.*


## What CSM Roles Actually Pay by Seniority


Customer Success Managers own the entire post-sale relationship: driving product adoption, managing renewals, spotting expansion opportunities, and acting as the internal voice of the customer inside their own company, according to[HubSpot's breakdown of the role](https://blog.hubspot.com/service/customer-success-manager) . That description covers an enormous range of actual jobs, though, and pay varies just as widely.


At the **associate or entry level** , expect a smaller book of accounts, closer supervision, and responsibilities weighted toward onboarding and support escalation rather than strategic account planning.[Built In's 2025 salary data](https://builtin.com/salaries/us/client-success-manager) shows entry-level client success pay sitting well below senior compensation, with substantial room for growth as scope expands. A **manager-level CSM** typically owns a defined book of mid-market or enterprise accounts, runs quarterly business reviews independently, and carries a renewal or expansion quota tied to[bonus pay and compensation trends](https://cs-recruiters.com/salary-guide/customer-success-manager) . **Senior and lead roles** shift further into strategy: Perforce's own senior manager posting lists ownership of net revenue retention targets, playbook creation for the broader team, direct people management, and cross-functional partnership with sales and product.


> **Salary snapshot:** Glassdoor's 2025 data shows New York City CSM pay running materially above many national medians, reflecting both cost of living and the concentration of well-funded tech and finance employers in the city. Total compensation for enterprise-level roles typically includes base salary plus a bonus tied to renewal and expansion targets, occasionally supplemented with equity at venture-backed companies.


When you get to the offer stage, negotiate more than just base pay:


- Bonus structure and the specific metrics it's tied to (gross retention vs. net retention vs. expansion revenue)
- Equity grants, especially at earlier-stage companies where base salary often runs lower
- Title, since "Senior CSM" versus "CSM II" can matter significantly for your next move
- Team size and reporting structure if the role includes any management scope


## Skills, Tools, and Resume Language That Get Callbacks


Hiring managers skim resumes looking for measurable outcomes, not job duties. "Managed a portfolio of accounts" tells them nothing. "Improved net revenue retention by driving renewal conversations across a $4M book of business" tells them everything they need to shortlist you.


Quantify wherever you can: retention percentage, expansion revenue or ARR growth, NRR or GRR improvement, time-to-value reduction during onboarding. If you don't have exact figures from a past role, approximate honestly rather than omitting the metric entirely. A rough number beats no number.


On the tools side, name the specific platforms you've used rather than generic categories. List CRM and customer success platforms by name, along with analytics tools (dashboards, health-scoring systems) and collaboration tools like Slack or Notion for cross-functional work. If you've worked with automation or AI-assisted workflows, say so explicitly. Hiring teams increasingly value candidates who understand[how AI tools accelerate operational work](https://skypher.co/post/advantages-of-ai-in-sales-b2b-success-en) , especially in tech and finance environments where efficiency directly affects margin.


A few resume bullet templates that tend to land well:


- "Owned a \[$X\] book of \[N\] enterprise accounts, achieving \[X%\] net revenue retention against a \[X%\] target."
- "Led onboarding redesign that cut time-to-first-value from \[X\] weeks to \[X\] weeks, reducing early churn by \[X%\]."
- "Built and scaled QBR cadence across \[N\] accounts, resulting in \[$X\] in expansion revenue over \[timeframe\]."


**Pro Tip:** *Link a redacted QBR deck or onboarding playbook in your application if the company allows portfolio attachments. Showing your work beats describing it, and it's one of the few CSM-specific artifacts that sets a candidate apart in a stack of otherwise similar resumes.*


On LinkedIn, mirror your resume's quantified language in your headline and About section rather than a generic "Customer Success professional" tagline. Recruiters search by keyword just as often as they browse, so specificity there compounds the effect of your resume.


## Application Checklist and Interview Preparation


Before you submit anything, run through a short pre-apply checklist: a resume tailored to the specific job description's language, a two-sentence note to any recruiter contact, a short cover note addressing why this company specifically, and any portfolio artifact relevant to the role's stage (early-stage onboarding focus versus mature enterprise retention focus).


Interview questions for CSM roles cluster around four scenarios almost every employer asks about:


1. **Onboarding** : "Walk me through how you'd structure the first 30 days for a new enterprise customer." Employers want to hear a repeatable process, not improvisation.
2. **Renewals** : "Tell me about a renewal you almost lost and how you saved it." This tests both instinct and process discipline under pressure.
3. **Escalation** : "Describe a time a customer was furious and how you de-escalated it." Hiring managers listen for ownership language, not blame-shifting.
4. **Expansion** : "How do you identify upsell opportunities without damaging trust?" This separates account managers from true strategic partners.


For the 30/60/90-day plan question, structure it differently depending on the employer type. An enterprise role calls for a plan weighted toward relationship mapping and account health diagnostics in the first 30 days. A scale-up or startup role calls for faster action: expect to be running your own QBRs by day 60 rather than day 90.


Timeline stage What typically happens Your move


Application to first response 1 to 2 weeks Follow up once if silent


First interview to offer 3 to 5 weeks, 3 to 4 rounds Ask about decision timeline in every round


Offer negotiation 3 days Negotiate bonus structure and title, not just base


## Why Skypher and Automation Experience Matter for CSM Hiring


Tech and finance employers hiring for customer success management jobs increasingly favor candidates who understand automation, not just relationship management. Security, compliance, and operational efficiency have become part of the CSM skill set in industries where trust and speed both drive revenue.


Skypher's own platform reflects exactly what these employers now expect a strong CSM candidate to understand: how[AI-powered automation](https://skypher.co/feature/ai-powered-recommendation-engine) reduces manual work across security questionnaires, how integrations with more than 40 third-party risk platforms streamline cross-team collaboration, and how[automated review cycles](https://skypher.co/feature/automated-review-cycles-and-duplicate-detection) cut the time it takes to close enterprise deals. A candidate who can speak fluently about automation's role in customer trust, not just in the abstract but with specifics, stands out immediately in tech and finance interviews.


> Candidates who can point to concrete experience with automation, integrations, and cross-functional coordination consistently perform better in interviews for enterprise CSM roles, because these are the exact operational skills hiring managers ask about when testing for scale-readiness.


If your background touches security questionnaires, compliance workflows, or GDPR-related SaaS operations, name that explicitly on your resume rather than folding it into generic "customer success" language. It's a differentiator, not a footnote.


- Mention specific automation platforms or workflows you've operated, not just "process improvement"
- Quantify time saved or error reduction where you have the numbers
- Reference cross-functional work with security, compliance, or sales engineering teams by name


## A Recruiter's-Eye View on Standing Out in This Market


Security and compliance fluency is the single most underused differentiator I see in CSM applications for tech and finance roles. Most candidates lead with soft relationship skills. Hiring managers in these sectors are scanning for people who can speak the language of trust and risk. Pair that with automation literacy, and you jump ahead of a stack of otherwise similar resumes. Apply broadly, but tailor your top five applications hard, then follow up with a specific, quantified note to the recruiter within a week.


> *— Gaspard*
